spec.cue: The view is wide and soft at the edges, with a sharp middle that is far blurrier than yours. Ultraviolet shows as blue, and movement glows.

fov.note: whole-animal field of view, honeybee and bee group figure

fovea.note: no record gives a sharp-middle scale; a person's value is kept

glow.note: the app's choice for how movement is shown

sat.note: colour is kept, with the UV shift set by the matrix

rate.note: the flicker limit of about 200 Hz is far above a person's, so time runs faster for the bee

topoS.note: by analogy with the sharper middle of the eye, drawn as an app choice

BEE.note: UV shown as blue, blue as green, green as red, red discarded; the app's convention for bee colour

rows: A honeybee can tell apart stripes only about a quarter of a cycle per degree apart. A person can see about 60 cycles per degree, so a bee sees roughly 1/230 as much detail. Bumblebees and stingless bees are similar, and the view shows the picture as very soft.
Bees see nearly all the way round, with a small blind spot behind and below. The eyes overlap only in front, so the picture is wide and flat at the edges.
A honeybee's eye can follow flicker up to about 200 flashes a second in bright light, far faster than a person's 60. The view runs at double speed to suggest this.
Bees see ultraviolet, blue and green, and no far red. The violet and blue tints in this view stand in for ultraviolet, and the app chose how to show it.
The app chose to make movement glow, because bees pick up motion strongly and it is the cue that the records describe most clearly.

claims.how: The honeybee worker behavioural limit is 0.26 cycles per degree.
Bees are given a field of view of about 300 degrees horizontally.
Honeybee flicker fusion of about 200 Hz against a person's near 60 Hz gives roughly a double rate; graded g because the person figure is not in the records.

quotes.quote: They found that the highest spatial frequency reliably resolved by the bees was 0.26 cycle deg−1, with no evidence of a difference in acuity between horizontal and vertical gratings.
Bees can see ~300° horizontally on the body plane with low spatial resolution for peripheral ommatidia
At ca. 200 Hz the FRC drops to 50%.
